sets.title: The fixation on metrics
sets.topic: Quản lý công · đo lường hiệu suất
sets.passage: Few administrative habits have spread as relentlessly as the urge to quantify. Hospitals, universities and police forces are now routinely assessed through performance indicators, on the assumption that what can be counted can also be improved. The economist Charles Goodhart observed as early as 1975 that once a measure is turned into a target, it ceases to be a reliable measure, because those being assessed learn to manipulate the figures rather than the reality behind them. His warning has been largely ignored. Critics such as Jerry Muller argue that the problem is not measurement itself but the fixation on it: numerical data, they contend, are indispensable when they inform the judgement of experienced practitioners, yet corrosive when they are used to replace it. Muller concedes that metrics have occasionally exposed genuine failings, notably in surgical outcomes, where publishing mortality rates prompted some underperforming units to reform. Nevertheless, he notes that the same publication led a number of surgeons to decline high-risk patients altogether, so as to protect their statistics.

items.stmt: {gd:Goodhart} was the [fi:first person] to [no:notice] that [tg:targets] can [ds:distort] measurement.

fi.vi: bài chỉ nói 'as early as 1975', không nói 'đầu tiên'

items.explain: 'Largely ignored' (phần lớn bị phớt lờ) = 'little influence' (ít ảnh hưởng). Đồng nghĩa → TRUE.

items.explain: 'Occasionally exposed' (đôi khi đã phơi bày) mâu thuẫn với 'never revealed' (chưa bao giờ). Bẫy: từ 'concedes' (thừa nhận) – Muller chấp nhận một phần điểm tốt của metrics.

items.explain: 'The same publication' = việc công bố tỉ lệ tử vong. 'Decline high-risk patients' = 'avoid treating dangerous cases' → TRUE.

sets.title: Rewriting the past: memory reconsolidation
sets.topic: Khoa học thần kinh · trí nhớ
sets.passage: For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists believed that a memory, once consolidated, was stored in a more or less permanent form, much as a document is filed in an archive. Experiments conducted around the turn of the millennium challenged this view. Researchers found that when rats were prompted to recall a fearful association, the memory temporarily became unstable, and administering a drug that blocked protein synthesis at that moment could weaken it substantially. Recollection, in other words, appeared to reopen a memory for revision before it was stored again – a process now termed reconsolidation. The implications are considerable. On the one hand, the finding offers a plausible mechanism for the well-documented unreliability of eyewitness testimony, since each act of remembering creates an opportunity for distortion. On the other, it has raised hopes that traumatic memories might be deliberately modified, although clinical trials have so far produced inconsistent results, and some ethicists have questioned whether altering a person's past experience is ever desirable.

items.stmt: Scientists once [th:thought] that a memory, after it had been {co:consolidated}, was essentially [g:____].
items.explain: 'Permanent form' → fixed (cố định). 'Inaccessible' (không truy cập được) sai nghĩa.

items.stmt: However, studies on {rt:rats} showed that [rc:remembering] a fearful event made the memory [g:____] for a [st:short period].
items.explain: 'Unstable' (không ổn định, dễ bị thay đổi) → vulnerable (dễ bị tổn thương/tác động).

items.stmt: This process may [ex:explain] why the [ac:accounts] given by [g:____] are often [ur:inaccurate].

ex.vi: cơ chế hợp lý (để giải thích)

items.explain: 'Eyewitness testimony' = lời khai của nhân chứng → witnesses. 'Scientists' là bẫy (có trong bài nhưng sai chỗ).

items.stmt: The research has also [en:given rise to] [g:____] that [tm:distressing memories] could be {md:deliberately modified},
items.explain: 'Raised hopes' → optimism (sự lạc quan). 'Scepticism' (hoài nghi) là trái nghĩa – nghĩ đến các nhà đạo đức học nhưng đó là ý khác.

items.explain: 'Inconsistent results' → mixed (lẫn lộn, lúc được lúc không). 'Conclusive' (có tính kết luận) là trái nghĩa.

sets.title: Why languages fall silent
sets.topic: Ngôn ngữ học · ngôn ngữ tuyệt chủng
sets.passage: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that as many as half may fall silent by the end of this century. The conventional explanation attributes this decline to globalisation, yet the historical record suggests a more complicated picture. Languages have always vanished; what is unprecedented is the pace. Moreover, the decisive factor is seldom outright prohibition. Far more often, parents in minority communities voluntarily abandon their ancestral tongue, reasoning that fluency in a dominant language will secure their children's prospects. This choice, rational at the level of the individual household, produces a collective loss that no single family intended. Revitalisation efforts have yielded mixed results. Hebrew, revived as an everyday language in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, is frequently cited as proof that extinction can be reversed, but its case is arguably exceptional: its revival coincided with the founding of a nation-state that had compelling ideological reasons to promote it. Communities lacking such institutional backing have generally found it far harder to persuade younger speakers that the effort is worthwhile.

items.stmt: What does the writer consider [un:new] about the [ls:disappearance] of languages today?

the speed at which it is happening

items.explain: 'Languages have always vanished' loại D. Cái mới (unprecedented) là 'the pace' = tốc độ → B.

a shortage of written materials

items.explain: 'Seldom outright prohibition' loại A. 'Far more often, parents ... voluntarily abandon' → B.

options: It is usually made under pressure from the authorities.
It makes sense for each family but has an effect nobody wanted.
It rarely benefits the children involved.
It is based on inaccurate information about the future.
items.explain: Câu 'rational at the level of the individual household, produces a collective loss that no single family intended' được paraphrase gần như toàn bộ trong B.

items.stmt: The writer refers to the [rs:restoration] of {hb:Hebrew} in order to
options: show that any language can be saved with enough effort
suggest that a well-known example may not be typical
criticise the methods used by the state
explain why young people reject minority languages
items.explain: A là quan điểm của người khác ('frequently cited as proof'); tác giả phản bác bằng 'but ... arguably exceptional' → B.

options: finding qualified teachers
competing with other minority languages
convincing the young that the effort is worthwhile
opposition from national governments
items.explain: 'Far harder to persuade younger speakers that the effort is worthwhile' → C.

sets.title: Learning from nature: biomimicry
sets.topic: Kỹ thuật · thiết kế mô phỏng sinh học
sets.passage: Engineers have long borrowed ideas from nature, but the deliberate, systematic study of biological solutions – now often called biomimicry – has gained momentum only in recent decades. Its advocates point to a growing list of successes. The structure of termite mounds, which maintain a remarkably stable internal temperature without any external energy source, informed the design of an office complex in Zimbabwe that uses a fraction of the electricity consumed by conventionally cooled buildings of similar size. The microscopic texture of sharkskin, which discourages bacteria from settling, has been reproduced on hospital surfaces. Critics, however, caution against romanticising the natural world. Evolution does not produce optimal designs; it produces structures that are merely adequate for an organism's survival, and these are constrained by the materials and developmental pathways available. A bird's wing, for instance, must also serve functions irrelevant to an aircraft. The most productive approach, these critics suggest, is not to copy nature directly but to extract the underlying principle and adapt it to human requirements.

items.stmt: Although engineers have {lb:long borrowed} ideas from nature, a [g:____] approach to this has [gm:become popular] [rc:only lately].

rc.vi: chỉ trong vài thập kỷ gần đây

items.explain: 'Deliberate, systematic' → methodical (có phương pháp). 'Commercial' không có trong bài.

items.stmt: An office building in {zb:Zimbabwe}, [ms:based on] {tm:termite mounds}, uses [fl:much less] [g:____] than [cp:comparable] buildings.
items.explain: 'Electricity' → power. 'Maintenance' (bảo trì) không được nhắc.

items.stmt: {cr:Critics} [wa:warn] that evolution creates designs that are [on:no more than] [g:____] for {sv:survival}.
items.explain: 'Merely adequate' → sufficient (vừa đủ). 'Perfect' bị phủ định bởi 'does not produce optimal designs'.

items.stmt: Such designs are also [lm:limited] by the [g:____] and developmental routes that are {av:available}.
items.explain: 'Constrained by the materials and developmental pathways available' → materials.

items.explain: 'Extract the underlying principle' → principle. 'Structure' là bẫy: có trong bài nhưng ở ý khác.

sets.title: The paradox of choice revisited
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · hành vi người tiêu dùng
sets.passage: In a frequently quoted experiment conducted in a Californian supermarket, shoppers who were offered a tasting table of twenty-four varieties of jam were considerably less likely to make a purchase than those offered only six. The finding seemed to confirm an intuition that had long circulated among marketing professionals: that an abundance of options can paralyse rather than liberate. Subsequent research, however, has proved difficult to reconcile with this tidy conclusion. A meta-analysis combining the results of some fifty studies found that the average effect of increasing choice was close to zero, with some experiments reporting the opposite pattern. Researchers have since attempted to identify the circumstances under which an excess of options does become burdensome. The effect appears strongest when consumers lack clear preferences, when the alternatives are difficult to compare, and when they are under pressure to decide quickly. Such qualifications are rarely mentioned in the popular books that have turned the original study into a parable about modern life.

items.stmt: The results of the {jm:jam} experiment [sp:came as a surprise to] [me:people in marketing].
items.explain: Kết quả 'confirm an intuition' (xác nhận trực giác vốn có) của dân marketing → không hề bất ngờ → FALSE.

items.stmt: [ls:Later studies] have [cs:consistently supported] the original finding.
items.explain: 'Difficult to reconcile with this tidy conclusion' + hiệu ứng trung bình gần bằng 0 → không ủng hộ nhất quán → FALSE.

items.stmt: {st:Some experiments} found that [mo:offering more options] had the [rv:reverse] effect.
items.explain: 'Some experiments reporting the opposite pattern' → TRUE.

items.stmt: [tc:Too much choice] is [ml:most likely] to cause difficulty when shoppers are [un:unsure what they want].
items.explain: 'The effect appears strongest when consumers lack clear preferences' → TRUE.

items.stmt: The [rs:researchers who ran the original study] [ob:object to] the way their work has been [po:popularised].

ob.vi: bài không nói ý kiến của nhóm nghiên cứu gốc

items.explain: Bài phê bình các cuốn sách phổ thông, nhưng không hề nói nhóm nghiên cứu gốc phản đối → NOT GIVEN. Đừng nhầm ý của TÁC GIẢ với ý của nhân vật khác.

sets.title: The ambiguous triumph of farming
sets.topic: Khảo cổ học · nguồn gốc nông nghiệp
sets.passage: The transition from foraging to farming, which began in south-west Asia roughly twelve thousand years ago, was long portrayed as a triumph of human ingenuity: once people grasped that seeds could be planted, the advantages of a settled life were supposedly so obvious that the new practice spread rapidly. Archaeological evidence now suggests a slower and more ambiguous process. Wild cereals were cultivated for well over a millennium before they display the physical changes associated with full domestication, and many communities moved back and forth between farming and foraging for generations. Nor were the benefits self-evident. Skeletal remains from early agricultural villages frequently show signs of nutritional deficiency and reduced stature compared with those of contemporary hunter-gatherers, while dense settlements encouraged the spread of infectious disease. Why, then, did farming prevail? One influential answer is that it supported higher population densities: even if individual farmers were less healthy, farming communities could simply outnumber their neighbours. Agriculture, on this view, succeeded not because it improved lives but because it multiplied them.

items.stmt: The [sh:shift] from foraging to farming was [lp:for a long time presented] as proof of human [g:____].
items.explain: 'Ingenuity' → inventiveness (óc sáng tạo).

items.stmt: It was [as:assumed] that the new practice had {sp:spread} in a [g:____] manner.
items.explain: 'Spread rapidly' → swift. 'Gradual' là bẫy: đó là quan điểm MỚI ('slower'), không phải quan điểm cũ được hỏi.

items.stmt: However, [sk:bones found] in early farming villages suggest that people there were often [g:____] and [sm:shorter] than hunter-gatherers.
items.explain: 'Nutritional deficiency' → malnourished (suy dinh dưỡng). 'Healthier' trái nghĩa.

items.stmt: In addition, [cr:crowded villages] helped [g:____] to {sp:spread}.
items.explain: 'Infectious disease' → illnesses.

items.stmt: Farming may have {pv:prevail}ed because it [ss:made possible] larger [g:____], even if {lh:individual farmers} were [hl:in poorer health].

g.vi: mật độ dân số cao hơn

items.explain: 'Higher population densities' / 'multiplied them' → populations. 'Harvests' (mùa màng) không được nhắc.

sets.title: A short history of peer review
sets.topic: Lịch sử khoa học · xuất bản học thuật
sets.passage: It is commonly assumed that peer review – the practice of submitting research to the scrutiny of independent experts before publication – has been a cornerstone of science since its origins. In fact, the system in its modern form is surprisingly recent. When the Royal Society began publishing its Philosophical Transactions in 1665, decisions about what to print rested largely with the editor, and for much of the following two centuries most journals operated on a similar basis. Systematic external refereeing became widespread only after the Second World War, when a dramatic expansion in the number of submissions made it impossible for editors to evaluate every manuscript themselves. Even the journal Nature did not adopt formal peer review for all its papers until the 1970s. Historians who draw attention to this chronology are not, for the most part, seeking to discredit the practice. Their point is rather that the authority now attached to it owes as much to institutional necessity as to any demonstrated ability to separate sound research from flawed.

items.explain: 'Has been a cornerstone of science since its origins' rồi bị phản bác bằng 'In fact ... surprisingly recent' → B.

independent specialists
the editor
the authors themselves
items.explain: 'Rested largely with the editor' → C. B (independent experts) là đặc điểm của peer review hiện đại – bẫy.

items.explain: Lý do nằm ngay sau 'when ...' → A. Các lựa chọn khác không được nhắc.

items.explain: Từ 'Even' cho thấy ngay cả tạp chí hàng đầu cũng áp dụng muộn → A.

sets.title: The ironies of automation
sets.topic: Công nghệ · tự động hóa và con người
sets.passage: Automation is usually justified on the grounds that machines are less prone to error than people. Yet the introduction of automated systems frequently creates a new category of mistake. Studies of pilots, radiologists and process-plant operators have documented a tendency, known as automation bias, for human supervisors to accept a system's recommendations without adequate scrutiny, even when contradictory information is readily available. Paradoxically, the more reliable a system is, the more pronounced this tendency becomes: operators who rarely see the machine fail gradually lose the habit of checking it. A related difficulty is the erosion of manual skills. When automation does break down, it typically does so in unusual circumstances that its designers failed to anticipate – precisely the situations in which an experienced human would be most valuable, and in which a deskilled one is least capable of intervening. Some researchers therefore advocate designs that keep operators actively engaged, for example by requiring them to perform certain tasks manually at regular intervals, even at some cost to efficiency.

items.explain: 'Less prone to error' → giảm inaccuracies (sai sót).

items.stmt: {su:Human supervisors} may {ac:accept} a system's [rc:advice] without proper [g:____].
items.explain: 'Scrutiny' → examination. 'Training' là bẫy: hợp ngữ pháp nhưng không có trong bài.

items.stmt: [pd:Strangely], this tendency becomes [wo:stronger] as systems become more [g:____].
items.explain: 'Reliable' → dependable. 'Complex' nghe hợp lý nhưng bài không nói.

items.explain: 'Unusual circumstances that its designers failed to anticipate' → unforeseen. 'Routine' trái nghĩa.

items.explain: 'At regular intervals' → periodically. 'Permanently' sai vì chỉ là thỉnh thoảng định kỳ.

sets.title: Why new roads fill up
sets.topic: Quy hoạch đô thị · giao thông
sets.passage: For much of the twentieth century, traffic engineers approached congestion as a straightforward problem of supply: if roads were overcrowded, the remedy was to build more of them. Yet a growing body of evidence indicates that additional capacity tends to generate additional traffic. When a new lane is opened, journeys that drivers previously avoided – because they were inconvenient, or could be made by public transport – suddenly become attractive, and within a few years the road is frequently as congested as before. This phenomenon, known as induced demand, was described in outline as early as the 1930s, but it was not until the 1990s that transport departments began to take it seriously in their forecasts. The converse also seems to hold. Studies of cities where major roads have been closed, whether through deliberate policy or as a result of disasters, report that a proportion of the displaced traffic simply disappears rather than overwhelming neighbouring streets. Such findings remain counterintuitive to many motorists, and politicians have generally been reluctant to act on them.

items.stmt: Twentieth-century {te:traffic engineers} [rg:treated] congestion as a [cx:complicated] problem.
items.explain: 'Straightforward' (đơn giản) trái nghĩa với 'complicated' → FALSE.

items.stmt: Adding [rc:road capacity] [of:often] leads to congestion [sb:returning to its earlier level].
items.explain: 'Frequently as congested as before' → TRUE.

items.stmt: {id:Induced demand} was [fi:first identified] in the {ys:1990s}.
items.explain: Đã được mô tả từ 1930s; 1990s chỉ là lúc được 'take seriously'. Bẫy: năm 1990s có trong bài nhưng gắn với ý khác → FALSE.

items.stmt: When major roads are {cl:closed}, [al:all of the traffic] moves onto [ns:nearby streets].
items.explain: 'A proportion of the displaced traffic simply disappears rather than overwhelming neighbouring streets' → không phải tất cả → FALSE.

items.stmt: Closures caused by {ds:disasters} have had [ml:longer-lasting effects] than [pl:planned closures].

ml.vi: bài không so sánh độ bền của tác động

items.explain: Bài nhắc cả hai loại đóng đường nhưng KHÔNG so sánh chúng → NOT GIVEN. Câu so sánh hơn mà bài không so sánh = dấu hiệu NG.

sets.title: In defence of boredom
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · quan điểm tác giả
sets.passage: Boredom has rarely enjoyed a good reputation. Moralists have long treated it as a symptom of idleness, and modern employers regard it chiefly as a threat to productivity. In my view, both attitudes misunderstand its function. Boredom is best understood not as an absence of stimulation but as a signal that our current activity has ceased to engage us meaningfully – in that sense it resembles pain, which is unpleasant precisely because it prompts us to act. Some psychologists have gone further, claiming that periods of tedium are a precondition for creativity. The evidence for this is suggestive rather than conclusive: laboratory studies in which participants who first completed a dull task subsequently generated more inventive ideas have proved difficult to replicate. What seems beyond dispute, however, is that the habit of reaching for a phone at the first hint of tedium deprives people of the opportunity to discover what they actually wish to do. Schools that schedule every minute of a child's day may therefore be doing more harm than good, though I would not go so far as to recommend that lessons be made deliberately monotonous.

items.explain: Tác giả nói 'both attitudes misunderstand its function' → không đồng ý với quan điểm truyền thống → NO.

items.stmt: The writer [cm:likens] {bo:boredom} to [ph:an unpleasant bodily feeling] that [mo:pushes us into action].
items.explain: 'It resembles pain, which is unpleasant precisely because it prompts us to act' → YES.

items.explain: 'I would not go so far as to recommend...' = tác giả KHÔNG khuyên như vậy → NO. Bẫy: từ 'recommend' có trong bài nhưng bị phủ định.

sets.title: The problem of the last mile
sets.passage: In freight logistics, the final stage of a journey – the movement of goods from a local depot to the customer's door – is notoriously the most expensive. Industry estimates commonly attribute more than half of total delivery costs to this 'last mile', largely because vehicles must make numerous small drops along unpredictable routes, often failing to find anyone at home. The rapid expansion of online retail has intensified the problem, while also generating congestion and emissions in residential streets that were never designed for heavy commercial traffic. Firms have experimented with a variety of remedies. Parcel lockers, located at stations and supermarkets, allow customers to collect items at their convenience and enable couriers to consolidate dozens of deliveries into a single stop. Some cities have established micro-hubs from which cargo bicycles complete the final leg, an approach that appears particularly effective in dense historic centres. Autonomous delivery robots have attracted considerable publicity, but their deployment remains confined to small trials, partly because regulators are uncertain how they should share pavements with pedestrians.

items.stmt: The {fs:final stage} of delivery is [kn:well known] to be the [g:____] part of the journey.
items.explain: 'Most expensive' → costliest. 'Slowest' không được nhắc.

items.stmt: This is [ma:mainly] because drivers make [nu:many small stops] and [of:frequently] discover that [g:____] are not at home.

g.vi: (không có) ai ở nhà = người nhận

sets.title: Science by the crowd
sets.passage: Over the past two decades, so-called citizen science – research in which members of the public collect or analyse data – has grown from a curiosity into a significant contributor to several disciplines. Amateur birdwatchers now supply much of the information used to track changes in bird populations, and online volunteers have classified millions of galaxy images that professional astronomers could never have examined unaided. Sceptics initially questioned the reliability of such data, arguing that untrained observers would inevitably make errors. Studies comparing volunteer and expert classifications have largely allayed these fears, provided that tasks are clearly defined and each item is examined by several participants, so that individual mistakes cancel one another out. A subtler concern is that projects tend to recruit from a narrow demographic: participants are disproportionately well educated and affluent, which may skew both the questions that are asked and the locations from which data are gathered. Proponents argue that the greatest benefit of citizen science may lie not in the data at all but in the scientific literacy it fosters, though this claim has so far received little systematic investigation.

sets.title: What happens to memories at night
sets.topic: Khoa học thần kinh · giấc ngủ
sets.passage: Scientists have long suspected that sleep plays a role in memory, but only recently have they begun to understand the mechanism. During deep, slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus – a structure that temporarily stores new experiences – appears to replay the day's events, transferring them to the cortex, where they are integrated with existing knowledge. Experiments in which volunteers learned word pairs before either sleeping or remaining awake have repeatedly found that those who slept recalled more the following morning. Intriguingly, sleep does not merely preserve memories; it seems to reorganise them. In one well-known study, participants who slept were more than twice as likely as those who stayed awake to discover a hidden rule that simplified a numerical task. Such findings have practical implications. Students who sacrifice sleep to revise late into the night may undermine the very learning they are trying to secure, and shift workers, whose sleep is frequently disrupted, may be at a particular disadvantage when acquiring new skills.

sets.title: The box that changed trade
sets.passage: Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was a slow and labour-intensive business. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels and crates of every size, and gangs of dockworkers stowed them by hand, a process that could keep a vessel in port for a week or more. The American trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean is generally credited with demonstrating that standardised steel boxes, which could be lifted directly from lorry to ship, would transform this process. His first converted tanker sailed from Newark to Houston in 1956. The economic consequences were not immediate. Ports had to be rebuilt with specialised cranes and vast storage areas, and dockworkers' unions, fearing mass redundancies, resisted the change for years. Only after international standards for container dimensions were agreed in the late 1960s did the system begin to spread worldwide. Economists still disagree about how much of the subsequent growth in world trade can be attributed to containerisation, but one widely cited study concluded that its effect was larger than that of all trade agreements of the period combined.

sets.title: A second life for batteries
sets.topic: Công nghệ · tái chế pin lithium
sets.passage: As electric vehicles multiply, attention is turning to what will happen to their batteries once they reach the end of their useful lives. Lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals such as cobalt, nickel and lithium, yet at present only a modest proportion are recycled, in part because their designs vary so widely between manufacturers that disassembly cannot easily be automated. The two dominant recovery methods each involve compromises. Pyrometallurgy, which smelts batteries at high temperatures, is robust and tolerant of mixed inputs, but it consumes large amounts of energy and loses much of the lithium. Hydrometallurgy, which dissolves the materials in chemical solutions, recovers a wider range of metals but generates liquid waste that must be carefully treated. A third option, known as direct recycling, attempts to restore the cathode material without breaking it down into its constituent elements; it promises substantial savings but remains largely confined to the laboratory. Many analysts argue that the most effective intervention would be regulatory: requiring manufacturers to standardise designs and label battery chemistry clearly would make every recycling method cheaper.

sets.title: When to trust your gut
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · trực giác chuyên gia
sets.passage: It is often said that experts rely on intuition rather than deliberate reasoning, and in many fields this description is accurate. An experienced firefighter may sense that a building is about to collapse without being able to explain why; a chess master may glance at a board and immediately see the strongest move. Yet I believe the popular enthusiasm for 'trusting your gut' has outrun the evidence. Intuition is reliable only in environments that are sufficiently regular and that provide rapid, unambiguous feedback, conditions that allow the patterns underlying expert judgement to be learned. Chess satisfies both requirements; long-term political forecasting satisfies neither, and it is no coincidence that the confident predictions of political pundits have been shown to be scarcely more accurate than chance. The difficulty is that subjective confidence is a poor guide to accuracy: an intuition feels equally compelling whether or not it rests on genuine expertise. Organisations would therefore be wise to ask not how certain their experts feel, but whether the domain in which they work is one in which skill can be acquired at all.

sets.title: Why cities run hot
sets.passage: On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island, arises chiefly because asphalt, brick and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after dark. Waste heat from air-conditioning units and vehicles adds to the effect, while the scarcity of vegetation deprives streets of the cooling provided by evaporation. The consequences are not merely a matter of discomfort. During heatwaves, mortality rates in dense urban districts have been found to exceed those in nearby rural areas, and the elderly are disproportionately affected. Remedies range from planting street trees to painting roofs in reflective colours, a measure that is cheap to implement although its benefits diminish as the paint becomes dirty. Some planners argue that such piecemeal interventions are insufficient and that the layout of cities must itself be reconsidered to allow cooling breezes to circulate.

sets.title: Farming upwards
sets.passage: Vertical farms grow crops in stacked layers inside buildings, using artificial light and nutrient solutions instead of soil. The principal obstacle is energy. Replacing sunlight with LEDs is expensive, and electricity typically accounts for the largest share of operating costs. As a result, the industry has concentrated on leafy greens and herbs, which grow quickly and command high prices, while staple crops such as wheat remain commercially unviable. Several prominent companies have collapsed in recent years, leading sceptics to conclude that the sector was overhyped; others maintain that falling LED prices will eventually make the model profitable.

sets.title: The press and the spread of ideas
sets.passage: It is tempting to credit the printing press with an immediate revolution in European thought. The reality was more gradual. For several decades after movable type was introduced in the mid-fifteenth century, printers concentrated on texts for which demand was already assured – religious works, legal handbooks and classical authors – because producing books required substantial capital and unsold copies could ruin a business. What printing did change, almost at once, was the reliability of texts. Manuscripts copied by hand accumulated errors with each generation, whereas a printed edition gave hundreds of readers in different cities an identical version, enabling scholars to compare and correct one another's work. Historians have argued that this standardisation, rather than any sudden increase in literacy, was the press's most profound early contribution. Literacy itself rose only slowly and unevenly, remaining largely confined to towns for well over a century.

sets.title: In praise of failed experiments
sets.topic: Khoa học · quan điểm tác giả
sets.passage: Scientific journals overwhelmingly publish studies that report positive results, and researchers know it. The consequence, I would argue, is a distorted picture of the evidence. When an experiment fails to find the effect it was looking for, the findings are frequently left in a drawer, so that other scientists, unaware of the attempt, may waste years repeating it. Worse, a literature composed mainly of successes can make weak effects appear robust. Some journals now accept papers on the basis of their design before the results are known, a reform I regard as the single most promising development in recent decades. Critics object that such journals will fill with uninteresting work. This concern seems to me exaggerated: a carefully designed study that finds nothing is not trivial, since knowing where an effect is absent is itself valuable. Nevertheless, I accept that funding bodies, which still reward striking discoveries, must change their priorities if the reform is to succeed.

sets.title: Maps that told stories
sets.passage: Medieval world maps were rarely intended as tools for navigation. Large examples, displayed in cathedrals, arranged the known world around Jerusalem and filled its margins with biblical scenes and legendary creatures, functioning more as encyclopaedias of belief than as guides for travellers. Yet these charts said almost nothing about the interior of continents, reflecting the priorities of the merchants who commissioned them. The gradual adoption of a mathematical grid of latitude and longitude, revived from ancient Greek geography in the fifteenth century, eventually allowed information from many sources to be combined on a single consistent framework, although accurate measurement of longitude at sea remained elusive until the eighteenth century.

sets.passage: Scattered across parts of the deep ocean floor lie potato-sized nodules rich in manganese, nickel and cobalt, metals in growing demand for batteries. The abyssal plains, they point out, are home to a surprising diversity of organisms, many of which have never been described, and some of which depend on the nodules themselves as a surface on which to live. Because life at these depths grows and reproduces extremely slowly, disturbed areas may take decades or even centuries to recover. Experiments in which small patches of seabed were ploughed in the 1980s still show clear signs of damage today. An international authority is negotiating regulations, but several countries have called for a pause until the ecosystems are better understood.

sets.title: The myth of panic
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · đám đông khi thảm họa

Where people do die in crowds, the cause is usually not panic but density: when too many people are packed into a confined space, pressure can build up to dangerous levels even if everyone behaves calmly. sets.title: The value of a street tree

Less easily measured are the psychological benefits: several studies have linked greener neighbourhoods with lower stress levels. sets.title: Why we remember unfinished tasks
sets.passage: In the 1920s the Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that waiters in a Berlin café could recall complicated orders perfectly until the bill had been paid, after which the details seemed to vanish from their minds. sets.passage: As keyboards and touchscreens have spread through classrooms, a number of education systems have reduced the time devoted to teaching handwriting, and several American states briefly removed cursive script from their curricula altogether. Other studies have found that young children who practise forming letters by hand recognise those letters more quickly. Not every attempt to replicate these findings has succeeded, and critics note that the laptop users in the note-taking studies were rarely trained in effective strategies. sets.title: In defence of small talk
sets.passage: Small talk has an undeservedly poor reputation. It is commonly dismissed as a waste of time, an empty ritual that people endure only because social convention demands it, and many self-help writers urge their readers to skip it in favour of 'deeper' conversation. I think this view rests on a misunderstanding of what such exchanges are for. Remarks about the weather or the traffic are not meant to convey information; they are a way of signalling goodwill and testing whether a longer conversation is welcome. Seen in this light, the predictability of small talk is not a weakness but its whole point, since it allows strangers to engage without risk. There is also some evidence that brief friendly exchanges, even with people we will never meet again, measurably improve our mood, although the studies so far have been small. None of this means that every conversation should remain superficial. But those who refuse small talk altogether may find that they rarely get the chance to have the deeper conversations they say they prefer.

sets.title: The myth of multitasking
sets.passage: Employers often list the ability to multitask among the qualities they look for, and many people describe themselves as skilled at it. The research suggests that this confidence is largely misplaced. What we call multitasking is, for most tasks that require attention, actually rapid switching between them, and each switch carries a small cost in time and accuracy. Studies in which participants alternate between, for example, classifying numbers and classifying letters consistently find that performance is slower than when the same tasks are done one after the other. Ironically, people who multitask most frequently in daily life tend to perform worse on such tests than occasional multitaskers, perhaps because they are more easily distracted. It would be wrong, though, to conclude that doing two things at once is always a mistake. Listening to music while running or folding laundry while talking on the phone works perfectly well, because one of the activities has become automatic. The problem arises only when both demand our conscious attention, which is precisely the situation in most offices.

sets.title: The case against car-free cities

Shop owners in several European cities have reported falling sales after car restrictions were introduced, although in other places trade recovered within a few years as the streets attracted more visitors on foot. More seriously, people with disabilities and those who work night shifts frequently depend on cars because public transport does not serve their needs. A policy that improves the city for the young and mobile while making it harder to reach for everyone else can hardly be called progressive. The solution, in my view, is not to abandon the idea but to introduce it gradually, with exemptions and with substantial investment in accessible transport before, rather than after, the restrictions take effect.

sets.title: Should science be slower?
sets.topic: Khoa học · phương pháp nghiên cứu
sets.passage: The pressure on researchers to publish frequently has produced an extraordinary volume of scientific papers, now well over two million a year. Some observers celebrate this as evidence of a thriving enterprise. I am less convinced. A substantial proportion of published findings, particularly in psychology and biomedicine, have failed to hold up when other laboratories attempted to repeat them, and it seems likely that the rush to publish is partly responsible. Researchers who must produce a steady stream of articles to secure funding and promotion have little incentive to spend years on a single careful study. The so-called 'slow science' movement proposes that universities should judge academics on the quality of a few contributions rather than the number of their publications. This seems to me sensible, although I suspect it will be resisted by the institutions that currently benefit from simple, countable measures of output. It would also be naive to assume that slower research is automatically better; careless work can be done at any speed.

sets.title: Tourism and fragile places
sets.passage: Every summer, images of crowded beaches and queues at historic monuments revive the debate about overtourism. Venice, Barcelona and Dubrovnik have all introduced measures to limit visitor numbers, ranging from entry fees to restrictions on cruise ships. Such measures are understandable, but I think they address the symptom rather than the cause. The real problem is not that too many people travel but that they travel to the same few places at the same few times, encouraged by social media and by airlines that concentrate routes on the most popular destinations. Spreading visitors more evenly, both across regions and across the seasons, would relieve the pressure on famous sites while bringing income to areas that currently receive little. Admittedly, some places are so fragile that any significant number of visitors damages them, and for these strict limits are unavoidable. Yet for most destinations, I would argue, the aim should be to manage tourism better rather than simply to have less of it.

sets.title: What GDP leaves out
sets.topic: Kinh tế học · đo lường phúc lợi
sets.passage: Gross domestic product was never intended to measure national well-being. Simon Kuznets, who developed the first official estimates for the United States in the 1930s, explicitly warned Congress that the welfare of a nation could scarcely be inferred from a measure of national income. Yet GDP growth has become the headline figure by which governments are judged, and I believe this has distorted policy. Unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives, which economists estimate would be worth a large fraction of GDP if it were paid, is not counted at all. Conversely, activities that most people would regard as harmful can raise GDP: the cost of cleaning up after an oil spill is added to output. Several alternative indicators have been proposed, combining income with measures of health, education and environmental quality. None is perfect, and critics rightly point out that combining such different things into one number involves arbitrary choices. But the solution is surely to report a range of indicators alongside GDP, not to continue treating a single statistic as a verdict on national success.

sets.title: Praise and motivation in schools
sets.passage: Over the past two decades, teachers have been widely encouraged to praise pupils for their effort rather than for their intelligence. The advice derives from research by the psychologist Carol Dweck, whose experiments suggested that children praised for being clever became reluctant to attempt difficult tasks, while those praised for working hard sought out challenges. Dweck herself has made this point in recent years. sets.title: Rewilding: hope or hype?
sets.passage: Rewilding, the idea of restoring ecosystems by reintroducing missing species and then largely leaving nature to its own devices, has captured the public imagination. The return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 is its most celebrated example, often credited with a chain of effects in which reduced numbers of grazing elk allowed riverside trees to recover. I share the enthusiasm, but I think the story has been told too neatly. Later studies have suggested that the recovery of vegetation was patchy and that other factors, including drought and human hunting of elk, played a part. Nor can the Yellowstone experience simply be transferred to the crowded landscapes of Europe, where large predators inevitably come into conflict with farmers. This does not mean that rewilding projects should be abandoned. Smaller interventions, such as allowing rivers to flood their natural plains or returning beavers to wetlands, have produced clear benefits at modest cost. sets.title: The science of rogue waves
sets.passage: For centuries, sailors told of solitary waves of enormous height appearing without warning in otherwise moderate seas, but oceanographers tended to dismiss these accounts as exaggeration. Standard models of wave behaviour predicted that a wave more than twice the height of its neighbours should occur perhaps once in ten thousand years at any given location. Scepticism ended on New Year's Day 1995, when a laser instrument on the Draupner gas platform in the North Sea recorded a wave twenty-six metres high amid waves averaging around twelve metres. Since then, satellite surveys have shown that such 'rogue waves' are far more common than the models implied. Researchers now believe that several mechanisms can produce them, including waves travelling against strong currents and the nonlinear interaction of wave groups, in which one wave draws energy from those around it. Predicting exactly when and where a rogue wave will form remains beyond current capabilities, but forecasters can now identify conditions under which they are more likely.

sets.title: Storing renewable energy
sets.passage: The rapid growth of solar and wind power has created a problem that was largely theoretical twenty years ago: how to supply electricity when the sun is not shining and the wind is not blowing. Lithium-ion batteries, whose cost fell by roughly ninety per cent between 2010 and 2020, now provide much of the short-term storage on electricity grids, smoothing out fluctuations over a few hours. They are less suited to longer gaps, such as a windless week in winter, because storing several days of electricity in batteries would be prohibitively expensive. For this purpose engineers are exploring other technologies. Pumped hydroelectric storage, in which water is pumped uphill when power is cheap and released through turbines when it is needed, is long established but depends on suitable geography. Newer options include converting surplus electricity into hydrogen, which can be stored for months, though much of the energy is lost in the conversion. Most analysts expect future grids to rely on a combination of methods rather than any single solution.

sets.title: The bystander effect revisited
sets.passage: In 1964 newspaper reports claimed that thirty-eight neighbours had watched or listened as a young woman, Kitty Genovese, was attacked outside her apartment in New York, and that none of them intervened. The case inspired the psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané to investigate what became known as the bystander effect: the tendency for individuals to be less likely to help when other people are present. Their laboratory experiments supported the idea, showing that participants who believed they were the only witness to an emergency responded faster than those who believed others were also present. Later investigations revealed, however, that the original newspaper account was seriously inaccurate; far fewer people had witnessed the attack, and at least one had called the police. More recently, researchers analysing hundreds of real conflicts recorded by security cameras in several countries found that at least one bystander intervened in about nine out of ten cases, and that the presence of more people actually increased the chance that someone would help.

sets.title: Self-driving cars and responsibility
sets.passage: Much of the public discussion of self-driving cars has focused on dramatic ethical dilemmas, such as whether a vehicle should swerve to avoid pedestrians at the risk of harming its passengers. Engineers working on the technology tend to regard these scenarios as unrealistic; in practice, they argue, an automated car will almost always do best simply by braking. The more pressing questions are legal. When a conventional car crashes, responsibility normally lies with the driver. If the vehicle is driving itself, it is less clear whether the fault belongs to the owner, the manufacturer or the company that wrote the software. Several countries have begun to address this. The United Kingdom, for example, has passed legislation stating that when a vehicle is operating in self-driving mode, the person in the driver's seat is not liable for its driving, and responsibility passes to an authorised company. Insurers have generally welcomed such clarity, but consumer groups worry that manufacturers may become reluctant to share the data needed to establish what went wrong.

sets.title: Light pollution and the night sky
sets.passage: A child born today in a large European or North American city may never see the Milky Way. sets.title: Behavioural nudges and pensions
sets.passage: Traditional economic theory assumes that people make choices that serve their own long-term interests, provided they have the relevant information. Behavioural economists have challenged this assumption, pointing to the powerful influence of inertia. A striking illustration comes from workplace pension schemes. When employees must actively choose to join a scheme, many never do so, even though employers contribute money on their behalf. When the default is reversed, so that workers are enrolled automatically unless they choose to leave, participation typically rises dramatically. After the United Kingdom introduced automatic enrolment in 2012, the proportion of eligible private-sector employees saving in a workplace pension rose from under half to more than eighty per cent within a few years. Such 'nudges' are attractive to governments because they are cheap and preserve freedom of choice. Critics argue, however, that they can be used to steer people in directions that benefit institutions rather than individuals, and that the contribution rates set by default may be too low to provide an adequate retirement income.

sets.title: Mapping the ocean floor

sets.title: Why we get songs stuck in our heads
sets.passage: Almost everyone has experienced an 'earworm', a fragment of music that repeats in the mind without any deliberate effort to recall it. Surveys suggest that more than ninety per cent of people have earworms at least once a week. They are usually triggered by recent or repeated exposure to a song, but they can also be prompted by a word, a situation or even a particular mood associated with a piece of music. Researchers at Durham University who analysed thousands of reported earworms found that the songs most likely to get stuck tended to have a fast tempo and a melody that was simple in its overall shape yet contained some unusual intervals. Although earworms are generally harmless, a minority of people find them distressing. Studies have found that chewing gum reduces their frequency, possibly because it interferes with the inner rehearsal of music, and that completing a demanding mental task, such as a difficult puzzle, can also help to dislodge them.

sets.title: Informal settlements and planning
sets.passage: Around a billion people worldwide live in informal settlements, neighbourhoods built without official permission, often on land that residents do not legally own. For much of the twentieth century, governments commonly responded by clearing such areas and relocating their inhabitants to new housing estates on the edges of cities. These programmes frequently failed. Residents found themselves far from the jobs, markets and social networks on which their livelihoods depended, and many drifted back to the city centre. Since the 1990s, planners have increasingly favoured upgrading settlements where they stand, providing water, drainage, electricity and paved paths while allowing residents to remain. Granting secure tenure, or legal rights to the land, is often considered central to this approach, since families who are not afraid of eviction are more willing to invest in improving their homes. Upgrading is not cheap, however, and in densely built areas installing new infrastructure may still require some houses to be demolished.

sets.title: Bird song and city noise
sets.topic: Sinh học hành vi · đô thị
sets.passage: Birds rely on song to attract mates and defend territories, so the constant low-frequency rumble of traffic presents them with a problem. Studies of great tits in several European cities found that urban birds sang at a higher pitch than their relatives in forests, apparently to avoid being drowned out by the noise. Other species have shifted their singing to quieter times of day; European robins in some noisy areas sing more at night. These adjustments come at a cost. Higher-pitched songs travel less far, and in some species females appear to prefer the lower notes that males in quiet areas produce. During the reduced traffic of the 2020 lockdowns, researchers in San Francisco found that white-crowned sparrows sang more softly and with a wider range of notes, suggesting how quickly birds respond when noise levels fall. Whether these changes reflect learning by individual birds or genuine evolutionary adaptation is still debated.

sets.title: Placebos without deception
sets.passage: The placebo effect, in which patients improve after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient, has traditionally been thought to depend on deception: the patient must believe the pill is real. Similar 'open-label' placebo trials have since been conducted for chronic back pain and fatigue, often with positive results. Researchers suggest that the ritual of treatment, including the attention of a doctor and the act of taking a pill, may itself trigger physical responses. Sceptics note that the benefits reported have mostly involved symptoms that patients rate themselves, rather than objective measures such as blood tests.

sets.title: Congestion charging
sets.topic: Giao thông · chính sách đô thị
sets.passage: Congestion charging, in which drivers pay a fee to enter the busiest parts of a city during peak hours, is one of the few transport policies that economists almost universally support. The principle is straightforward: road space at rush hour is scarce, and charging for it encourages people to travel at other times, use public transport or combine trips. When London introduced its charge in 2003, traffic in the zone fell by around fifteen per cent in the first year and delays were substantially reduced. Stockholm's experience is particularly instructive. The city held a seven-month trial in 2006, during which public opinion, initially hostile, became markedly more favourable as residents saw the reduction in queues. A referendum then approved the charge permanently. Critics argue that such schemes fall most heavily on lower-income drivers, although supporters respond that the poorest households are the least likely to own cars, and that revenue can be used to improve buses and trains.

sets.title: The physiology of altitude
sets.passage: At the summit of Mount Everest, the air contains only about a third as much oxygen as at sea level, and most climbers rely on bottled oxygen to reach it. The human body adapts to altitude in several ways. Within hours, breathing becomes faster and deeper; over days and weeks, the body produces more red blood cells, increasing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen. This process, known as acclimatisation, is why mountaineers ascend gradually, spending nights at intermediate camps. Ascending too quickly can cause altitude sickness, ranging from headaches and nausea to life-threatening swelling of the brain or lungs. Populations who have lived at high altitude for thousands of years show distinctive adaptations. Many Tibetans, for example, carry a gene variant that limits the overproduction of red blood cells, which in other people can thicken the blood dangerously. Researchers believe this variant may have been inherited from the Denisovans, an extinct group of ancient humans.

sets.title: Ghost fishing gear
sets.passage: Every year, a large quantity of fishing equipment is lost or abandoned at sea. Nets, lines and traps made from durable synthetic materials can continue to catch fish, turtles, seabirds and marine mammals for years after they have been discarded, a phenomenon known as ghost fishing. Estimates suggest that abandoned gear makes up a substantial proportion of the large plastic debris floating in the ocean. Gear is lost for many reasons, including storms, entanglement on the seabed and conflicts with other vessels, and some is deliberately dumped, particularly where disposal facilities in ports are expensive or unavailable. Solutions under discussion include marking gear so that it can be traced back to its owners, offering payments to fishermen who return old nets to port, and developing biodegradable materials that break down more quickly. Several organisations also employ divers to recover lost nets, some of which are recycled into products such as carpets and clothing.

sets.title: Decision fatigue
sets.topic: Tâm lý học · ra quyết định
sets.passage: The idea that making many decisions in a row gradually wears down our ability to choose well has become popular in business and self-help literature. A frequently cited study of parole hearings in Israel found that judges granted parole in around two thirds of cases at the start of a session but in almost none just before a meal break, after which the rate of favourable decisions rose again. The authors interpreted this as evidence of mental fatigue, with tired judges falling back on the default option of refusal. The study has, however, been heavily criticised. Other researchers pointed out that the order of cases was not random: prisoners without legal representation, whose applications were less likely to succeed, tended to be heard later in each session. The broader theory that self-control relies on a limited mental resource that is used up has also struggled in replication attempts. Even so, few psychologists doubt that people sometimes make poorer choices when they are tired or hungry.

sets.title: Microfinance reassessed
sets.passage: Microfinance, the provision of small loans to people too poor to borrow from conventional banks, was once hailed as a revolutionary tool against poverty. Its best-known pioneer, Muhammad Yunus, founded the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh in 1983 and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006. Lending was typically organised through small groups of women, who were jointly responsible for repayment, a system that produced remarkably high repayment rates. By the late 2000s, however, enthusiasm had begun to fade. Six carefully designed randomised studies in different countries, published together in 2015, found that access to microcredit allowed some households to expand small businesses but had no significant effect on average household income. In some regions, rapid commercial expansion led borrowers to take loans from several lenders at once, resulting in crises of over-indebtedness. Most researchers now view microfinance as a useful financial service, particularly for managing irregular income, rather than as a route out of poverty in itself.

sets.title: Remote work and innovation
sets.topic: Quản trị · làm việc từ xa
sets.passage: The shift to remote work that began in 2020 has proved more durable than many managers expected, and a large share of office employees in wealthy countries now work from home for part of the week. Studies of productivity have produced mixed findings. Employees often report fewer interruptions and appreciate saving time on commuting, and some carefully measured studies of individual tasks, such as processing calls, have found small gains. However, there is growing concern about effects on collaboration and innovation. An analysis of communication patterns among tens of thousands of employees at a large technology company found that working remotely caused networks to become more static and isolated, with fewer connections between different groups. Such cross-group contact is thought to be an important source of new ideas. Junior staff may also lose out, since they learn a great deal from informal observation of experienced colleagues. Many organisations have therefore settled on hybrid arrangements, requiring attendance on particular days when teams can meet in person.

sets.title: Seed banks
sets.topic: Nông nghiệp · đa dạng sinh học
sets.passage: Since the beginning of agriculture, farmers have developed thousands of varieties of crops adapted to local soils, climates and pests. Over the twentieth century, much of this diversity was lost as farmers around the world switched to a small number of high-yielding varieties. Seed banks aim to preserve what remains. It holds duplicate samples from gene banks around the world as a back-up against disasters. This function was tested in 2015, when researchers whose collection in Syria had been disrupted by war withdrew seeds from the vault to rebuild it elsewhere. Seed banks have limitations. Seeds of some species, including many tropical trees, cannot survive drying and freezing, and stored seeds do not continue to adapt to changing conditions as crops growing in farmers' fields do.

sets.title: Searching for exoplanets
sets.passage: The first planet orbiting a Sun-like star outside our solar system was confirmed in 1995, and more than five thousand such exoplanets are now known. Because planets are tiny and faint beside their stars, astronomers rarely see them directly. The most productive technique, the transit method, detects the slight dimming of a star's light when a planet passes in front of it; NASA's Kepler telescope found thousands of planets this way. Another method measures the small wobble a planet's gravity causes in its star, which shifts the star's light slightly towards blue or red. Combining the two allows astronomers to estimate a planet's density and so to judge whether it is rocky or gaseous. Many of the planets discovered so far are unlike anything in our solar system, including 'hot Jupiters', giant planets orbiting closer to their stars than Mercury does to the Sun. The next major goal is to analyse the atmospheres of smaller rocky planets for chemical signs of life.
